comment: Agent SoW subcontracting (agentsow.com 0.18.0-draft, 5.15): who actually does the work, under what rule, and the chain rule that makes depth safe by induction - disclosure flattens upward, and terms only narrow going down. Pins the bytes and the branches where two implementations drift: the three-posture closed set (none / disclosed / approved), the clause shape (an entry names a party ON THE MESH - agent key, handle, or published role - and the vocabulary deliberately offers no free-text field for an off-mesh organisation, for the same reason the 12.1 qualification vocabulary has no probe kind a runtime cannot check: a disclosure nobody can look up, vouch, rate, or hold to account is decoration wearing disclosure's clothes; scope is required and bounded; a 'none' clause naming delegates is refused as self-contradictory; the grade is 'evidence', flatly), and the FLOW-DOWN COMPARATOR subcontractConformance / subcontract_conformance: one pinned sentence per violation, byte-identical across SDKs, empty where every checkable term narrows correctly - including terms met exactly, because narrowing includes staying put. Each term is checked only where the prime states it (a prime that says nothing constrains nothing), and 'states' is structural: whether a clause validates is the validators' question at document validation, never smuggled into the comparison. The jurisdiction set rides the confidentiality clause as processed_in (the chain rule's 'touch no jurisdiction the link above did not'); the clause validators do not model it yet and the comparator reads declared structure. THE FIXTURE IS THE AUTHORITY: when a test against it fails, fix the implementation; when the fixture itself is believed wrong, change it only with a spec change alongside.
spec: Agent SoW 0.18.0-draft: 5.15 (subcontracting), 5.11 (the confidentiality terms that flow down), 5.12 (the reporting levels that flow down), 5.5.3 (the cap the remainder is measured against), 12.1 (the on-mesh-only argument), 4.2 (grades)

postures.comment: 5.15: three postures, a closed set. Under 'none' the provider performs the work itself - and on a mesh where delegation forms engagements, on-mesh delegation under 'none' is discoverable evidence, not an argument. 'disclosed' permits delegation with every subcontractor named before its work begins. 'approved' additionally requires the client's countersigned approval per subcontractor, riding the same two-seat machinery amendments use. Absence states nothing: a document without this clause has said nothing about delegation either way, and a reader MUST NOT infer a posture.
postures.grade_why: 5.15 grades this clause flatly. Not 'enforced': the claim that nothing was delegated off-mesh is a statement about conduct beyond the mesh's sight, with breach as its consequence rather than detection as its guarantee. Not 'recorded': on this mesh delegation forms engagements the platform holds, which is more than a record of the clause.

clause.comment: The clause shape. subcontractors is REFUSED under posture 'none' (a none clause naming delegates contradicts itself) and optional under the disclosing postures - a clause with nobody named yet OMITS the member, and an empty list is refused as a second spelling of that omission. Each entry names at least one of agent / handle / role and carries the required scope. Backstops: at most 16 entries; agent and role up to 64 characters, handle up to 120, scope up to 300; no duplicate agent, no duplicate handle. An entry MAY carry `engagement`, the S4.1 identifier of the countersigned engagement the delegation runs under - the pin. Optional, because S5.15 also serves plain disclosure; a runtime that requires pins says so itself rather than the document carrying a flag about it.

conformance.comment: The flow-down comparison (5.15's chain rule): does the subcontract narrow every checkable term of the engagement above it? An EMPTY violations array means the chain narrows correctly. Violations arrive one pinned sentence each, in a pinned order - confidentiality promises in the closed vocabulary's declared order, then retention, then each stray jurisdiction in the sub's declared order, then reporting, then the cap - and the wording is part of the fixture: a provider refused a subcontract reads one message whichever SDK computed the chain. 'opts' carries prime_cap_remaining where the case supplies it; only the platform holding the money knows the remainder, so no opts means no cap check. A prime document of {} states nothing and constrains nothing; a sub of null declares nothing and violates exactly the terms the prime states (except reporting's honest records_only floor, which silence meets).
